questions.question: How old is your child or teen?
questions.hint: Optional — used for copy and relevance, not scoring.

options.label: 8 to 10
College-age but still living at home
Other

questions.question: What made you take this quiz today?

options.label: Setting screen limits has turned into a constant fight.
They're pulling away from us, and screens are where they disappear.
Sleep, bedtime, or mornings now revolve around the device.
Their mood rises and falls with likes, streaks, group chats, or social drama.
Gaming or online worlds seem to matter more than anything offline.
The content itself feels intense: anger, outrage, drama, or nonstop stimulation.
Money keeps coming up: in-game purchases, loot boxes, betting, or trades.
I'm not sure. Something just feels off.

questions.question: When you try to set a limit, what usually happens?

options.label: It turns into a fight, even when I try to stay calm.
There's always one more round, one more episode, one more thing they need to finish.
They seem crushed or unreachable, like I took away the only thing that was helping.
They sneak it, hide it, downplay it, or make it sound like less than it is.
They're annoyed, but they can usually stop.
Honestly, I avoid setting the limit because I can't handle another blow-up.
We have limits that mostly work.

questions.question: When is screen use hardest to interrupt?

options.label: Late at night, especially in bed.
First thing in the morning.
Before homework, chores, schoolwork, or anything hard.
After school or after a stressful day.
When they're bored, waiting, or between things.
When they're alone, left out, or disconnected.
When a group chat, game, stream, or online event is happening.
There's no clear pattern. It feels like all the time.

questions.question: If you had to guess, what is the screen giving them?
questions.hint: What it's really for, even if you're not sure.

options.label: A way to calm down, shut off, or not think for a while.
A place where they feel good at something.
Their people: friends, servers, fandoms, creators, or a world where they feel known.
Proof that they're included, liked, noticed, or not missing out.
A version of themselves or a world that feels better than real life right now.
Intensity, drama, edge, anger, or something that makes them feel awake.
The chance of a win, drop, reward, deal, trade, pull, or score.
I honestly don't know.

questions.question: After screen time goes too long, what do you notice?

options.label: They're exhausted, hard to wake, or the next morning is rough.
They're irritable, wired, or easier to set off.
They seem smaller, more self-conscious, or upset by social stuff.
They seem blank, numb, or checked out.
They're defensive or secretive when I ask what happened.
They're calmer for a little while, but the same need comes back.
I don't notice much afterward.

questions.question: Where is this costing your child or your family lately?

options.label: Sleep or mornings.
School, homework, chores, or responsibilities.
Mood, irritability, stress, or emotional swings.
Family conflict, trust, or the relationship between you.
Offline friends, activities, sports, hobbies, or leaving the house.
Self-image, appearance stress, comparison, or social confidence.
Money, purchases, bets, trades, or charges.
Secrecy, sneaking, lying, or hiding.
My own stress as a parent.
Nowhere meaningful, honestly.

questions.question: What role have you fallen into as the parent?

options.label: The phone police. I enforce, they resist, and we repeat.
The detective. I check, monitor, investigate, or try to catch what's happening.
The negotiator. Everything becomes a deal, exception, or argument over minutes.
The peacekeeper. Sometimes I give in because I need the house to calm down.
The fixer. I keep researching tools, controls, rules, and expert advice.
The worried observer. I can see something is off, but I don't know how to reach them.
The collaborator. We can usually talk about it and adjust.

questions.question: In the past month, which of these have been true?

options.label: We tried rules or limits, and they didn't really stick.
They keep going after a clear stopping point.
They get restless, anxious, angry, or very off when they can't use it.
They hide, sneak, downplay, or lie about use.
Sleep or mornings are clearly affected.
School, responsibilities, or offline life are clearly affected.
Money, charges, risky purchases, betting, or trading are involved.
I have a serious safety concern, like unsafe contact, exploitation, self-harm content, violence, or abuse.
None of these.
